b7.notes:
### 1. Fundamental Angle Relationships * **Complementary Angles:** Two angles whose sum equals exactly $90^\circ$: $$\theta_1 + \theta_2 = 90^\circ$$ * **Supplementary Angles:** Two angles whose sum equals exactly $180^\circ$ (angles on a straight line): $$\theta_1 + \theta_2 = 180^\circ$$ * **Vertically Opposite Angles:** When two straight lines intersect, the non-adjacent opposite angles are equal: $$\angle A = \angle B$$ * **Angles at a Point:** The complete rotation of angles around a single point sums to $360^\circ$: $$\sum \theta = 360^\circ$$
🔍 Self-Check: Complement vs. Supplement (Click to inspect) > **Question:** An angle measures $62^\circ$. Find its complement and its supplement. > > **Explanation:** > * **Complement:** $90^\circ - 62^\circ = \mathbf{28^\circ}$ > * **Supplement:** $180^\circ - 62^\circ = \mathbf{118^\circ}$
--- ### 2. Perimeter & Circumference of Circles * **Perimeter:** The total continuous distance around the outer boundary of a 2D plane shape. * **The Circle Ratio ($\pi$):** Pi is defined as the constant ratio of a circle's circumference ($C$) to its diameter ($d$): $$\pi = \frac{C}{d} = \frac{C}{2r} \approx \frac{22}{7} \approx 3.142$$ * **Circumference Formula:** $$C = 2\pi r = \pi d$$ --- ### 3. Area of a Triangle Every triangle is exactly half of a bounding rectangle or parallelogram sharing the same base $b$ and perpendicular height $h$: $$\text{Area of Triangle} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{perpendicular height} = \frac{1}{2}bh$$

workedExamples.problem:
In the road intersection diagram, an angle of $135^\circ$ forms a straight line with an angle marked $A^\circ$:

<svg viewBox="0 0 320 120" width="100%" height="110" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="my-2"><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="160" y1="90" x2="240" y2="20" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M 190 90 A 30 30 0 0 0 181 69" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/><text x="195" y="80" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">A°</text><path d="M 130 90 A 30 30 0 0 1 181 69" fill="none" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2"/><text x="135" y="80" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">135°</text><circle cx="160" cy="90" r="4" fill="#0f172a"/><text x="155" y="105" font-size="11" fill="#64748b">O</text></svg>

Determine the numerical value of angle $A^\circ$.
steps: Step 1 (Why we do this: Identify the geometric relationship): Angles on a straight line are supplementary and sum to $180^\circ$.

Step 2 (Why we do this: Set up the linear angle equation): 
  $$135^\circ + A = 180^\circ$$

Step 3 (Why we do this: Subtract 135° from both sides to isolate A): 
  $$A = 180^\circ - 135^\circ = 45^\circ$$

workedExamples.title: Circumference of a Circular Track
workedExamples.problem:
A circular roundabout has a radius of $140\text{ cm}$. Taking $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$, calculate:
(i) Its diameter.
(ii) Its circumference.
steps:
Step 1 (Why we do this: Diameter is twice the radius): 
  $$d = 2r = 2 \times 140\text{ cm} = 280\text{ cm}$$

Step 2 (Why we do this: Apply the circumference formula C = 2πr): 
  $$C = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 140$$

Step 3 (Why we do this: Cancel common factor 7 into 140): 
  $$C = 2 \times 22 \times 20 = 44 \times 20 = 880\text{ cm}$$

b8.notes:
### 1. Parallel Lines & Transversals

When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal line:
* **Corresponding Angles (F-Pattern):** Are equal.
* **Alternate Angles (Z-Pattern):** Are equal.
* **Co-Interior Angles (C-Pattern):** Sum to $180^\circ$.

---

### 2. Interior Angle Sum of an $n$-Sided Polygon

Any polygon with $n$ sides can be divided into $(n - 2)$ triangles from a single vertex:
$$\text{Sum of Interior Angles} = (n - 2) \times 180^\circ$$
* For a **Regular Polygon** (all sides and angles equal), each interior angle is:
  $$\text{Each Interior Angle} = \frac{(n - 2) \times 180^\circ}{n}$$
* **Exterior Angles Theorem:** The sum of exterior angles of **any** convex polygon is always $360^\circ$.

---

### 3. Area of a Circle

By slicing a circle into sectors and rearranging them into a pseudo-rectangle of length $\pi r$ and width $r$:
$$\text{Area of Circle} = \pi r^2$$

---

### 4. The Pythagorean Theorem

In any right-angled triangle, the area of the square on the **hypotenuse** ($c$, the longest side opposite the $90^\circ$ right angle) equals the sum of the areas of the squares on the other two sides ($a$ and $b$):
$$a^2 + b^2 = c^2$$
$$c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}, \quad a = \sqrt{c^2 - b^2}, \quad b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2}$$

#### Standard Pythagorean Triples to Memorize:
* $(3, 4, 5)$
* $(5, 12, 13)$
* $(8, 15, 17)$
* $(7, 24, 25)$
* $(9, 40, 41)$

b9.notes:
### 1. Primary Trigonometric Ratios (SOH CAH TOA)

In a right-angled triangle with reference angle $\theta$:
* **Hypotenuse ($H$):** The longest side opposite the $90^\circ$ right angle.
* **Opposite ($O$):** The side facing directly across from angle $\theta$.
* **Adjacent ($A$):** The side adjacent (next to) angle $\theta$, connecting it to the right angle.

$$\sin \theta = \frac{\text{Opposite}}{\text{Hypotenuse}} = \frac{O}{H}$$
$$\cos \theta = \frac{\text{Adjacent}}{\text{Hypotenuse}} = \frac{A}{H}$$
$$\tan \theta = \frac{\text{Opposite}}{\text{Adjacent}} = \frac{O}{A}$$

---

### 2. Angles of Elevation & Depression

* **Angle of Elevation:** The angle measured **upward** from the horizontal eye line to an object above.
* **Angle of Depression:** The angle measured **downward** from the horizontal eye line to an object below.
* **Geometric Equivalence:** Because horizontal reference lines are parallel, the **angle of depression equals the alternate angle of elevation**:
  $$\text{Angle of Depression} = \text{Angle of Elevation}$$

---

### 3. Surface Area & Volume of 3D Prisms

* **Surface Area of a Cuboid:**
  $$\text{TSA} = 2(lw + lh + wh)$$
* **Total Surface Area of a Cube:**
  $$\text{TSA} = 6s^2$$
* **Volume of a Cuboid / Rectangular Bucket:**
  $$\text{Volume} = l \times w \times h$$
* **Surface Area of a Triangular Prism:**
  $$\text{TSA} = 2(\text{Triangular End Area}) + \sum (3 \text{ Rectangular Faces})$$

workedExamples.problem:
The total surface area of a solid cube is $384\text{ cm}^2$. Calculate:
(i) The length of one side of the cube.
(ii) The volume of the cube.
steps:
Step 1 (Why we do this: A cube has 6 identical square faces): 
  $$\text{TSA} = 6s^2 = 384$$

Step 2 (Why we do this: Divide by 6 to find area of one face s²): 
  $$s^2 = \frac{384}{6} = 64$$

Step 3 (Why we do this: Take square root to determine side length s): 
  $$s = \sqrt{64} = 8\text{ cm}$$

Step 4 (Why we do this: Compute volume V = s³): 
  $$V = s^3 = 8^3 = 8 \times 8 \times 8 = 512\text{ cm}^3$$

### 1. Fundamental Angle Relationships * **Complementary Angles:** Two angles whose sum equals exactly $90^\circ$: $$\theta_1 + \theta_2 = 90^\circ$$ * **Supplementary Angles:** Two angles whose sum equals exactly $180^\circ$ (angles on a straight line): $$\theta_1 + \theta_2 = 180^\circ$$ * **Vertically Opposite Angles:** When two straight lines intersect, the non-adjacent opposite angles are equal: $$\angle A = \angle B$$ * **Angles at a Point:** The complete rotation of angles around a single point sums to $360^\circ$: $$\sum \theta = 360^\circ$$
🔍 Self-Check: Complement vs. Supplement (Click to inspect) > **Question:** An angle measures $62^\circ$. Find its complement and its supplement. > > **Explanation:** > * **Complement:** $90^\circ - 62^\circ = \mathbf{28^\circ}$ > * **Supplement:** $180^\circ - 62^\circ = \mathbf{118^\circ}$
--- ### 2. Perimeter & Circumference of Circles * **Perimeter:** The total continuous distance around the outer boundary of a 2D plane shape. * **The Circle Ratio ($\pi$):** Pi is defined as the constant ratio of a circle's circumference ($C$) to its diameter ($d$): $$\pi = \frac{C}{d} = \frac{C}{2r} \approx \frac{22}{7} \approx 3.142$$ * **Circumference Formula:** $$C = 2\pi r = \pi d$$ --- ### 3. Area of a Triangle Every triangle is exactly half of a bounding rectangle or parallelogram sharing the same base $b$ and perpendicular height $h$: $$\text{Area of Triangle} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{perpendicular height} = \frac{1}{2}bh$$

jhs2.notes:
### 1. Parallel Lines & Transversals

When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal line:
* **Corresponding Angles (F-Pattern):** Are equal.
* **Alternate Angles (Z-Pattern):** Are equal.
* **Co-Interior Angles (C-Pattern):** Sum to $180^\circ$.

---

### 2. Interior Angle Sum of an $n$-Sided Polygon

Any polygon with $n$ sides can be divided into $(n - 2)$ triangles from a single vertex:
$$\text{Sum of Interior Angles} = (n - 2) \times 180^\circ$$
* For a **Regular Polygon** (all sides and angles equal), each interior angle is:
  $$\text{Each Interior Angle} = \frac{(n - 2) \times 180^\circ}{n}$$
* **Exterior Angles Theorem:** The sum of exterior angles of **any** convex polygon is always $360^\circ$.

---

### 3. Area of a Circle

By slicing a circle into sectors and rearranging them into a pseudo-rectangle of length $\pi r$ and width $r$:
$$\text{Area of Circle} = \pi r^2$$

---

### 4. The Pythagorean Theorem

In any right-angled triangle, the area of the square on the **hypotenuse** ($c$, the longest side opposite the $90^\circ$ right angle) equals the sum of the areas of the squares on the other two sides ($a$ and $b$):
$$a^2 + b^2 = c^2$$
$$c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}, \quad a = \sqrt{c^2 - b^2}, \quad b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2}$$

#### Standard Pythagorean Triples to Memorize:
* $(3, 4, 5)$
* $(5, 12, 13)$
* $(8, 15, 17)$
* $(7, 24, 25)$
* $(9, 40, 41)$

workedExamples.problem: Calculate the size of one interior angle of a regular hexagon ($6$ sides).
steps:
Step 1 (Why we do this: Apply the polygon interior sum theorem for n = 6): 
  $$\text{Sum} = (n - 2) \times 180^\circ = (6 - 2) \times 180^\circ = 4 \times 180^\circ = 720^\circ$$

Step 2 (Why we do this: Divide by the number of equal vertices in a regular polygon): Since a regular hexagon has 6 identical interior angles:
  $$\text{Each Angle} = \frac{720^\circ}{6} = 120^\circ$$

<svg viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" height="140" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="my-2"><rect x="40" y="20" width="240" height="100" rx="6" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="40" y1="120" x2="280" y2="20" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="4"/><text x="130" y="65" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">Diagonal c = 41 in.</text><text x="120" y="136" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#334155">Width a = 40 in.</text><text x="285" y="75" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Height h = ?</text><rect x="265" y="105" width="15" height="15" fill="none" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.5"/></svg>

Calculate the vertical screen height $h$.
steps: Step 1 (Why we do this: Model the screen as a right-angled triangle): The diagonal forms the hypotenuse $c = 41\text{ inches}$. The width is $a = 40\text{ inches}$. The height is $h = b$.

Step 2 (Why we do this: State the Pythagorean relationship): 
  $$h^2 + 40^2 = 41^2$$

Step 3 (Why we do this: Isolate h²): 
  $$h^2 = 41^2 - 40^2 = 1,681 - 1,600 = 81$$

Step 4 (Why we do this: Take the principal square root): 
  $$h = \sqrt{81} = 9\text{ inches}$$

jhs3.notes:
### 1. Primary Trigonometric Ratios (SOH CAH TOA)

In a right-angled triangle with reference angle $\theta$:
* **Hypotenuse ($H$):** The longest side opposite the $90^\circ$ right angle.
* **Opposite ($O$):** The side facing directly across from angle $\theta$.
* **Adjacent ($A$):** The side adjacent (next to) angle $\theta$, connecting it to the right angle.

$$\sin \theta = \frac{\text{Opposite}}{\text{Hypotenuse}} = \frac{O}{H}$$
$$\cos \theta = \frac{\text{Adjacent}}{\text{Hypotenuse}} = \frac{A}{H}$$
$$\tan \theta = \frac{\text{Opposite}}{\text{Adjacent}} = \frac{O}{A}$$

---

### 2. Angles of Elevation & Depression

* **Angle of Elevation:** The angle measured **upward** from the horizontal eye line to an object above.
* **Angle of Depression:** The angle measured **downward** from the horizontal eye line to an object below.
* **Geometric Equivalence:** Because horizontal reference lines are parallel, the **angle of depression equals the alternate angle of elevation**:
  $$\text{Angle of Depression} = \text{Angle of Elevation}$$

---

### 3. Surface Area & Volume of 3D Prisms

* **Surface Area of a Cuboid:**
  $$\text{TSA} = 2(lw + lh + wh)$$
* **Total Surface Area of a Cube:**
  $$\text{TSA} = 6s^2$$
* **Volume of a Cuboid / Rectangular Bucket:**
  $$\text{Volume} = l \times w \times h$$
* **Surface Area of a Triangular Prism:**
  $$\text{TSA} = 2(\text{Triangular End Area}) + \sum (3 \text{ Rectangular Faces})$$

workedExamples.problem:
The angle of depression of a stone from the top of an observation tower to the ground is $45^\circ$:

<svg viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="100%" height="150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="my-2"><line x1="60" y1="30" x2="160" y2="30" stroke="#64748b" stroke-dasharray="4" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="60" y1="30" x2="60" y2="130" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="4"/><text x="10" y="85" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Tower (h = ?)</text><line x1="40" y1="130" x2="280" y2="130" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="3"/><text x="105" y="148" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#334155">Ground Distance = 120m</text><line x1="60" y1="30" x2="240" y2="130" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M 100 30 A 40 40 0 0 1 93 48" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/><text x="105" y="45" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">45° (Depression)</text><path d="M 200 130 A 40 40 0 0 1 206 111" fill="none" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2"/><text x="155" y="122" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">45° (Elevation)</text><circle cx="240" cy="130" r="5" fill="#e11d48"/><text x="248" y="130" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#e11d48">Stone</text></svg>

If the stone is $120\text{ metres}$ away from the base of the tower, find the height of the tower. (Take $\tan 45^\circ = 1$).
steps: Step 1 (Why we do this: Convert angle of depression to angle of elevation via alternate interior angles): The horizontal line from the tower top is parallel to the ground, so the angle of elevation from the stone to the tower top is also $45^\circ$.

Step 2 (Why we do this: Select the trigonometric ratio linking opposite and adjacent): In the right triangle, height $h$ is opposite to $45^\circ$ and ground distance $120\text{ m}$ is adjacent:
  $$\tan 45^\circ = \frac{\text{Opposite}}{\text{Adjacent}} = \frac{h}{120}$$

Step 3 (Why we do this: Substitute known value tan 45° = 1 and solve for h): 
  $$1 = \frac{h}{120} \implies h = 120 \times 1 = 120\text{ metres}$$

workedExamples.title: Cube Surface Area and Volume Deduction
workedExamples.problem:
The total surface area of a solid cube is $384\text{ cm}^2$. Calculate:
(i) The length of one side of the cube.
(ii) The volume of the cube.
steps:
Step 1 (Why we do this: A cube has 6 identical square faces): 
  $$\text{TSA} = 6s^2 = 384$$

Step 2 (Why we do this: Divide by 6 to find area of one face s²): 
  $$s^2 = \frac{384}{6} = 64$$

Step 3 (Why we do this: Take square root to determine side length s): 
  $$s = \sqrt{64} = 8\text{ cm}$$

Step 4 (Why we do this: Compute volume V = s³): 
  $$V = s^3 = 8^3 = 8 \times 8 \times 8 = 512\text{ cm}^3$$

hard.prompt: The total surface area of a right triangular prism is $120\text{ cm}^2$. The triangular cross-section has base $3\text{ cm}$, height $4\text{ cm}$, and hypotenuse $5\text{ cm}$. What is the prism length $L$?
hard.hint: Two ends $= 2(\frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 4) = 12$. Perimeter $= 3 + 4 + 5 = 12$. Set $12 + 12L = 120$.
hard.workedSolution:
$$\text{Two triangle bases} = 2 \times 6 = 12\text{ cm}^2$$
$$\text{Lateral Area} = 120 - 12 = 108\text{ cm}^2$$
$$\text{Perimeter} = 3 + 4 + 5 = 12\text{ cm}$$
$$L = \frac{108}{12} = 9\text{ cm}$$.
